sources.title: How do I dispute a charge on my credit card bill? (Fair Credit Billing Act)
supports: Written billing-error dispute notice must reach card issuer within 60 days after first statement showing the charge
Card issuer must acknowledge in writing within 30 days and resolve within two billing cycles (no more than 90 days)
sources.reverification: Re-read 2026-10-23: 60 calendar days for the written billing-error notice and 30 days for the acknowledgment. Page reviewed APR 15, 2024.

sources.publisher: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau / eCFR (National Archives) - Regulation Z
sources.title: 12 CFR § 1026.13 — Billing error resolution
supports: (b)(1): the billing-error notice must reach the creditor no later than 60 days after the first periodic statement reflecting the error.
(c)(1): written acknowledgment within 30 days of receiving the notice.
(c)(2): resolution within 2 complete billing cycles and in no event later than 90 days.
sources.why_added: The 60-day / 30-day figures are on the CFPB consumer page, but the 2-billing-cycle / 90-day outer limit is not. That limit is in this section, so it is now cited to the section itself.

sources.publisher: U.S. Federal Trade Commission / eCFR (National Archives)
sources.title: 16 CFR Part 23 - Guides for the Jewelry, Precious Metals, and Pewter Industries
supports: § 23.3(a): it is unfair or deceptive to misrepresent the presence, quantity or karat fineness of gold in a product, or the fineness, thickness, weight ratio or manner of application of any gold plating
§ 23.3(b): examples of misleading 'gold' usage for coated, plated, filled, overlay and electroplated products

§ 23.3(c)(1): using 'Gold' for a gold-alloy product with a hollow centre may mislead unless the hollow centre is disclosed immediately beside the word; such products 'should not be marked or described as solid'
§ 23.18: misrepresentation of weight and 'total weight' (section heading read in the part's table of contents)
sources.caveat: The eCFR itself states the displayed content is 'authoritative but unofficial'; the official CFR print edition remains the legal reference.

sources.title: Buying Platinum, Gold, and Silver Jewelry
supports: Karat is parts of pure gold out of 24 (18K = 18 parts gold to 6 parts other metal; 14K = 14 to 10)
'Solid gold' means the item is not hollow and carries a karat mark

Definitions of gold plated, gold filled, gold overlay, rolled gold plate (RGP), gold electroplate, vermeil, gold flashed, gold washed
Check a seller's refund and return policy and get it in writing; search the seller's name with 'complaint' or 'review'
sources.reverification: Re-read 2026-10-23: karat-out-of-24 definition, quality-mark-plus-trademark rule, 'solid gold' = not hollow, and the plated/filled/overlay/RGP/electroplate/vermeil definitions all still present.

sources.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology (nist.gov)
sources.title: NIST Handbook 44 — Current Edition (2026): Specifications, Tolerances, and Other Technical Requirements for Weighing and Measuring Devices
supports: The live 2026 Handbook 44 index page was read; it links every section (1.10 General Code, 2.20 Scales, 2.21 … 2.25, Section 3 device codes) as DOCX/PDF.
The index page itself does NOT print a troy-ounce or metric-carat conversion factor, so no numeric factor is attributed to it by this project.
sources.correction_2026_10_23: The previously registered URL https://www.nist.gov/pml/owm/metric-publications/nist-handbook-44 was re-opened on 2026-10-23 and returned NIST's own 'Page not found' (error 404). It also carried the invented-looking subtitle 'Appendix C: Units of Mass for Precious Metals & Metric Carat', which is not what the page says. Both were replaced.

sources.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
sources.title: NIST Special Publication 811 — Guide for the Use of the International System of Units (SI)
supports: 'carat, metric → gram' is listed as 2.0 E-01 in bold (= exact) in Appendix B.8, i.e. 0.200 g exactly.
'ounce (troy or apothecary) → gram' is listed as 3.110 348 E+01 and is NOT bold, i.e. 31.10348 g rounded, not an exact table value.
sources.correction_2026_10_23: This project uses 31.1034768 g per troy ounce, which is the 480-grain definition (480 × 64.79891 mg) and agrees with NIST's rounded table entry. It must not be quoted as 'NIST's exact conversion factor'. The earlier supports text did exactly that and has been corrected; the constant itself is unchanged and still exact by definition.

sources.publisher: U.S. Code (Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School) - 15 U.S.C. § 1666
sources.title: 15 U.S.C. § 1666 — Correction of billing errors (Fair Credit Billing Act)
supports: (a)(A): the creditor must send a written acknowledgment within 30 days of receiving the billing-error notice, unless it completes the correction in that period.
(a)(B): the creditor must correct the account or send a written explanation within two complete billing cycles and in no event later than 90 days.
(a)(B)(ii): where the goods were never delivered, the creditor cannot treat the amount as correctly shown unless it determines the goods were actually delivered.
sources.why_added: The two-billing-cycle / 90-day limit and the 30-day acknowledgment are statutory here. The catalog cites § 1666; this registry entry gives that citation a verified page. Read directly on 2026-10-23 by this session.

sources.publisher: U.S. Code (Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School) - 15 U.S.C. § 295
sources.title: Standard of fineness of gold articles; deviation
supports: Actual fineness of the assayed part may not be more than 0.003 below the stamped fineness
Actual fineness of the entire article including solder may not be more than 0.007 below the stamped fineness (articles other than watchcases and flatware)
sources.caveat: LII reproduces the U.S. Code; the official text is published by the U.S. House (uscode.house.gov) and GPO.
sources.reverification: Re-read 2026-10-23: three one-thousandth parts tolerance for the part assayed, seven one-thousandth parts for the whole article including solder.

sources.publisher: U.S. Code (Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School) - 15 U.S.C. § 297
sources.title: 15 U.S.C. § 297 — Stamping plated articles
supports: Subsection (b): a person applying a quality mark to a gold or silver article must also apply a trademark registered in the U.S. (or their name), in lettering at least as large as the quality mark and as close as possible to it.
Subsection (a): plated articles must not be stamped 'sterling' or 'coin'.
sources.why_added: standards.html cited 15 U.S.C. § 297 for the hallmark-plus-trademark rule, but no sources.json entry existed, so the citation had no registry backing. Added after reading the section on 2026-10-23.
